item.title: how to do test-driven development
item.description:
The runtime unit is the use case

rule
the runtime unit is the use case, never the feature.
  • why: a use comes in whole sessions — triaging a morning’s photos, running the cabinet frame, picking a few shots to send — and those sessions are the propositions the program makes.
  • why: a test written per feature asserts a proposition nobody holds, since nobody opens a program in order to exercise one button.
rule
one function per session runs its whats in the order the person performs them, carrying state from step to step.
  • why: a chain of gestures on one open program is what using it looks like, and an isolated one-gesture run is a path no human takes.
rule
every session is one somebody really lives.
  • how: the user tells the stories and the agent never invents one.
  • how: the agent writes the what, the how and the tests, and assembles them into the stories it was told.
  • why: there are very few of them, because a session is a whole real use rather than a feature.
rule
a test names the promise it verifies.
  • why: everything else a test could check is a measure of a proposition the program makes.
  • rule: a test with no promise to name is deleted rather than filed.
rule
between them the stories reach every promise the program makes.
  • why: a promise no story reaches goes unmeasured.
  • how: the agent finds the gap and must propose it; the user decides.
  • how: a what that fits no session is that signal — either a story is missing from the set, or nobody does that thing, and which it is is the user’s call.
rule
ground walked twice is cut.
  • why: it is time spent measuring a promise already measured.
  • how: the agent suggests the stretch to cut and the user cuts it.
  • scope: stories overlap a little whatever happens, each one opening the program and loading the same first screen, and that much is irreducible.
  • scope: the user may bend a story so that it stops short of showing the whole thing, when per is confident the trimmed part is measured elsewhere.
    • why: what is protected is semantic coverage, not the walking of every path.
rule
a block joins the session where it still bites.
  • why: the session is the proposition, the blocks are its measures, and the document owes the reader the entailment between them.
  • how: each block must still fail observably once the earlier steps have run before it.
  • how: a block whose failure an earlier step masks belongs to another session.
[Step, not measure]: a block that cannot fail without an earlier block failing with it is a step, not a measure.
+> [Pinned upstream]: the promise such a block appears to pin is pinned upstream.
+> [Prose attributes it upstream]: the prose names the block that actually pins the promise, not the step.
+> <Drop the step>: a step measures nothing, so it comes out of the session. <- [State it leaves behind]: the session may need the state it leaves behind.

[No verdict distinguishes them]: no verdict tells you whether a block is a step or a measure.
+ [One outcome for all]: a session reports one outcome for all its blocks, so pure setup and pure measurement are the same colour from outside.
+> <Undecidable>: no verdict distinguishes them, so which is which cannot be known. <- [Read it off the text]: which blocks earn their slot as steps is read off the text, by asking of each what would die if only this one were wrong.
<- <Instrument the silent block>: a block that never turns out to be the one that failed is the signature to look for, and it is worth instrumenting.

<Instrument the silent block> <- [A candidate, not an answer]: the signature hands you a candidate, not an answer.

The cycle is the unit of change

rule
the cycle is the unit of change.
  • why: each step exists because the previous one is provably insufficient.
  • why: skipping a step leaves a gap the next regression will fall into.
rule
the baseline run covers the whole suite.
  • why: a subset baseline proves only that subset was green, and says nothing about pre-existing reds elsewhere.
  • why: a red lit by the post-change run then cannot be dated — your change, or already broken before you started.
  • why: a subset baseline reads green while the codebase is red, and that comfort is what makes later regressions hard to date.
  • why: after a whole-suite baseline, every red observed was caused by the change in flight.
rule
a codebase that is red and not flaky has its tests fixed before the task at hand resumes, unless the user explicitly asks otherwise.
rule
the subset whose violation would invalidate the product runs on every cycle.
  • scope: which properties those are is a per-project decision; re-asserting them is not.

Red proves the test

rule
a test that has never been observed failing has not been observed.
rule
the test is written first and watched failing before any production code changes.
  • why: that failure is what establishes that the test exercises the new behaviour.
  • why: without it, a passing test proves only that the assertion compiles — the path it claims to cover may already be wired, or the assertion silently vacuous.
rule
the failure mode and message are part of the test’s value.
rule
reverting the change makes the test fail again.
  • why: a red observed once is a fixed point, and failing again confirms the test rides on the new code.
  • why: a test that cannot be made to fail by reverting the change is testing nothing in particular.
rule
a test that was restructured rather than written earns its red again, by breaking the behaviour it names and watching it fail.
  • why: a restructuring starts and ends green, so the moment that would have shown the test still bites never arrives.
  • why: a check that quietly stopped checking anything is indistinguishable, in a green suite, from one that works — the count of passing tests reads the same.
  • why: the failure names which check catches the break, so a check that has drifted to where an earlier one already covers it is visible as well.
  • how: break one behaviour at a time, in the production code, and require the named check to be the one that fails; a break nothing catches is a check that promises what it does not read, and a break something else catches first is a check whose promise is kept elsewhere.
rule
a promise that cannot be broken from where the suite stands is recorded as such, in the prose, with the reason.
  • why: otherwise it is indistinguishable from one nobody has got round to breaking, and the next reader spends the effort again.
  • why: the reason is itself a finding — it usually names a boundary the suite cannot reach past, which is worth knowing before trusting what lies beyond it.

Minimum to green, then earn the next line

rule
new behaviour appears under a failing test, and the next test earns the next line.
  • why: code beyond what the failing test demands is untested by definition.
  • why: the coupling keeps the suite a faithful description of the system, every branch tracing back to a test that was once red.
  • scope: a refactor pass adds structure no single test motivates.
  • rule: an anticipated edge case is written as the next failing test, not as a preemptive guard in the current change.

The whole suite is the contract

rule
a change is verified only when the whole suite is green.
  • why: the new test going green proves the new behaviour exists, and says nothing about what the change broke elsewhere.
  • why: implicit dependencies between modules — shared state, cached values, ordering assumptions — surface only when every test runs.
  • why: the test you left out is the one most likely to catch the regression you did not predict.
  • why: confidence scoped to a subset is scoped to the regressions you already imagined, and the value of the suite is the ones you did not.
rule
no whole-suite run is substituted by a faster subset.
  • why: a green-to-green refactor can still flip a subtle ordering, a fixture, or a shared helper.
  • why: what each run guards against is unknown ahead of time, which is what makes it a regression rather than an anticipated case.

Refactor lives under green

rule
structural change runs under a green suite.
rule
behaviour is held fixed by the tests, and structure is the only thing allowed to move.
  • why: mixing behaviour change with structure change loses the bisect signal — a test going red mid-refactor no longer tells you whether it caught a regression or reacted to an in-progress edit.
rule
the tests are refactored with the same discipline.
  • why: tests are code, and they duplicate, drift and slow down.
  • why: the refactor-tests step is the only place in the cycle where test debt can be paid without losing signal, the suite being green on both sides of the edit.
  • why: a suite that takes too long stops being run.
  • why: a suite full of duplicated assertions gives false confidence that coverage is broader than it is.

Tests live at the seam the user touches

rule
assertions probe the observable surface — visible text, public API, exported artifact, ARIA role — not internals like private stores, test-only hooks or implementation-selector classes.
  • why: a test coupled to internals breaks on every refactor and stops being a contract, becoming a tax that punishes structural improvement.
  • how: the suite reaches for get_by_role, get_by_label and get_by_placeholder rather than CSS selectors that encode the current DOM.
    • why: writing user-level helpers is paid back the first time a refactor changes the markup without changing the behaviour.

A test seeds the world it reads

rule
a test creates the rows it depends on, asserts only on what it created, and removes them again.
  • why: what decides whether a test is reproducible is who put its data there.
  • why: data the environment happened to hold — a live row, a value from a shared dump, a label that was there last month — is state no one pinned.
  • why: a change made elsewhere, a renamed label or a pruned row, then turns the test red with no edit to the code it guards, and the red points at the wrong place.
  • why: a failure that moves on its own is worse than no test.
  • scope: a shared fixture may stand the environment up — a database, a server, a seeded dump — and the test still adds the value it needs, exercises it, and tears it down.
    • why: the green then rides on the code under test and nothing else.
rule
a test loose at either end has stopped being a contract.
  • scope: the in end is its own fixtures, never the ambient world; the out end is the user’s surface, never internals.

Test, don’t patch

rule
every fix earns a test — written first, observed red, then made green by the smallest change that satisfies it.
  • why: without a test that captures the bug, the fix is invisible to the suite — no proof the bug existed, no proof it is gone, no defense against its return.
  • why: a bug fix landed without a test recurs, and leaves no record of why the line was added.
  • scope: this is the cycle applied to regression rather than feature work — the bug report is the what, the failing test its translation, the fix the minimum code that turns it green.

A flake is a diagnosis, not a knob

rule
an intermittent red is measured before any limit is touched.
  • why: widening a timeout until it goes quiet raises the threshold at which the cause shows, trading a signal for a longer wait.
  • why: the expected time usually sits far under the ceiling, so the failure is a transient — a CDN stall, a resource race — to remove or isolate.
rule
a timeout is raised only when the measurement shows the expected time nearing it.
  • rule: the new number is justified in a comment.
rule
flakiness that is not obvious to fix earns meaningful logging.
  • why: it helps investigate the next time the flakiness occurs.
rule
moving on a flaky test is the choice of the user, never yours.

Cycle prompt

rule
any edit runs through the cycle below.

Audit prompt

rule
in code, the audit is a table — every observation cited by file and line, classified under the principle it tests.
rule
the conclusion follows from the table, not alongside it.
authority
the general rule that an observation is cited rather than asserted lives in how to write and audit a note.

item.title: how to make a PWA install as a WebAPK
item.description: On Android the same PWA can install two very different ways. One is a real app: its own icon in the launcher, its own entry in the system’s app settings, no browser chrome, and it captures links into its scope. The other is a bookmark wearing a small Chrome badge that reopens in a tab. The first is a WebAPK, the second a shortcut. Which one you get is not a user choice — it is a verdict Chrome passes on your manifest at install time. This note is the recipe for earning the WebAPK verdict, distilled from getting score counter tally to mint one after it sat stuck as a shortcut for months.

how to write a literature note
item.description:
Table of Contents
  • The objective is the contract
  • Neutrality is key
  • The chain runs from objective to answer
  • The reader’s flow is sacred
  • Every semantic claim is an Argdown node
  • Off-topic is exclusion, not appendix
  • Source quality is part of the claim
  • Notes linking here
  • Permalink

The objective is the contract

A literature note answers one stated question. The question is written before any other prose — it is the contract the rest of the note has to honour. A reader scanning the note must be able to tell, in one line, what the note is going to settle and what it is not. Without that contract, the note becomes a dump: there is no test for whether a given paragraph belongs.

The objective also bounds the work. A note finishes when its question is answered, not when the source has been read in full. Material that is interesting but off-topic earns its own note with its own objective; appending it here would dilute the contract this note is going to be audited against. Hereafter, audit refers to the act of reading the note carefully and checking it against each of the rules that follow.

Neutrality is key

Neutrality starts upstream of the prose, in the formulation of the objective itself. A question — “what does the spec require for X?” — admits any answer the source supports. A thesis dressed as a question — “why does the spec require X?” — has already chosen the answer, and every step downstream inherits the choice: what is read carefully, what is quoted, how the quote is paraphrased. The independent reader does not catch this, because they can only check the quotes the author selected, and the author selected to confirm. The objective is therefore phrased as an open question, and any framing that presupposes its own answer is rewritten before the source is opened.

The chain runs from objective to answer

Sections follow the path the reader needs to take from the question at the top to the conclusion at the bottom. Each one moves the argument by exactly one step: it introduces the next concept the answer depends on, or rules out a candidate the objective could have been confused with. A section that does neither is noise, regardless of how interesting it is in its own right.

The order of sections is not the order in which the reading of the source happened. The note is rewritten, after the source is digested, so the chain is the shortest path from objective to answer. If a detour was needed during research and is not needed in the final argument, it is dropped — its absence in the chain is the audit. A reader who has to reconstruct the argument from a meandering note is doing the work the note was supposed to do.

This chain is made explicit as an Argdown map, not left to prose: each statement and each inference is a node wired by a typed relation, and the prose only narrates the map (the node discipline is three kinds, nothing else; the relation vocabulary and tooling are in argdown in org-mode).

The reader’s flow is sacred

The reader should glide through the prose uninterrupted, clicking through to a claim’s source node whenever they want to verify it against the original. Everything else — detours, meta-commentary, secondary justifications — is noise and must be removed. If something is valuable but breaks the flow — a side comparison, a self-contained derivation whose result the argument will consume — move it to its own note and link to it from the main chain at the moment its result is used.

Brevity serves flow. The longer a sentence, the more its message dilutes — attention is narrow, and a convoluted clause already costs a glance back. Where a bulleted breakdown carries the idea more directly than a paragraph, prefer it.

Put a lot of links — to the canonical source URL of a cited text, to the matching map node. If the reader wants to follow a concept referred to and described somewhere else, they must be able to simply click and go there.

A new term enters the document where the document has just laid out what motivates it — not earlier. In a literature note this rule is acute, because the source vocabulary is dense and indexical: article numbers, case identifiers, doctrinal labels, regulatory acronyms. A section title like « 666 plutôt que 653 » breaks flow on the heading itself, because the reader has not yet been told what each one says or why one might apply. The fix is to name the question instead — « quelle présomption s’applique au grillage ? » — and let the identifier arrive in a sentence the body has already prepared. When the structure constrains the sequence, defer the reference: name the general concept the reader already has, and let the specific identifier arrive when its time comes. The rule applies everywhere the reader’s eyes go — section titles, body sentences, node titles, link anchors.

A literature note is a story, not an inventory. Three elements carry rigorous content through:

  • stakes — the open question;
  • tension — the chain of arguments building toward a result;
  • payoff — the answer, or a documented unresolved disagreement.

The reader should feel the writer’s pull toward the answer; substance without narrative rarely lands.

Every semantic claim is an Argdown node

Every claim, every argument, every conclusion is a node in the Argdown map, wired by a typed relation; the prose only narrates the map. There are three kinds of node, and nothing else:

  • sourced statement — a verbatim quote of its source: the node carries + [source] and reproduces the exact words, the source text living in its own node with the canonical link. Such a quote node earns its place only by atomising — lifting out of a longer source the single proposition the argument uses; when the source node is itself already that lone proposition, a separate quote node merely copies it, and the argument cites the source node directly.
  • argument — a PCS: premises → ---- → conclusion, the inference holding literally — if the premises, read to the letter, do not entail the conclusion, cut it (« il s’ensuit que » rescues nothing).
  • conclusion — the output of a PCS, or a premise that is the author’s own reading, explicitly marked unsourced.

Never an interpretation as a sourced node: a reading, gloss, qualification or inference is a conclusion or a flagged unsourced premise, never a node carrying + [source] as if the source had said it. One node = one atomic claim — so a verbatim quote that only restates a source node already pared to that single claim is not a node of its own but a copy, and collapses into a direct citation of that source. Anything neither sourced nor derived this way is a guess and does not belong.

Prose may carry an affirmation the map does not — a framing line, a bridging remark the chain never formally consumes as a node. This is allowed, but it does not escape sourcing: any such out-of-map affirmation takes a footnote holding the verbatim source and a link to the reference, exactly as a source node would. The footnote is the prose counterpart of the source node — same verbatim discipline, same canonical link. An affirmation stated outside the map and without that footnote is a bare guess in the narrator’s voice; it is footnoted or cut, never left standing.

Off-topic is exclusion, not appendix

Material that does not move the chain from objective to answer is cut, even when it is correct, even when it was hard-won during the reading. A literature note is not a record of what was read; it is the distilled answer to one question. A reader who scanned the objective and is looking for the answer must not have to skip past unrelated paragraphs to find it.

Sourced is not load-bearing. A correct, well-cited fact whose removal would not weaken the chain — a foundational article cited for atmosphere, a date that no later sentence consumes, a parenthetical clarification — earns no place by being true. The test is consequence: if the paragraph still follows when the sentence is deleted, the sentence was not chain-bearing and is cut. The same test applies to source nodes; an orphaned source node is the fingerprint of an orphaned claim and goes with it.

The cut material is not lost: it earns its own note, with its own objective, and is linked from any chain where it is actually load- bearing. This is also how the note set grows without each individual note becoming a swamp. A note that tries to hold every adjacent fact ends up holding none of them well, and the link graph between notes — which is where the value compounds — never forms.

Source quality is part of the claim

A source node pointing at the primary source — the specification, the standard, the maintainer’s own documentation, the source code of the system under discussion, or a blog post or forum answer from a well-known and respected actor of the domain — supports a claim differently than one pointing at a forum thread or a blog post by an unknown author. Both are citations; only one is evidence. The note prefers the primary source whenever it exists and is reachable, and names it as such.

Secondary sources are admissible only when they interpret a primary source the note cannot host — paywalled, deprecated, untranslated — and they are named as secondary, with the reason the primary is not cited directly. Anonymous forum posts, undated blog entries, screen- shots without provenance, and AI-generated summaries are not citations: they are unsourced claims wearing the costume of one, and they do not survive the audit. A note built on them collapses the moment the sourcing chain is followed.

The channel matters as much as the source. Each intermediary between the note and the source — a search engine, a reformatter, a third-party mirror, a cache — is a place where wording can drift or the wrong version can be served. A dedicated channel the source itself exposes — an official API, a structured archive addressable by a canonical identifier (Legifrance for French legal texts, an MCP tool for an agent) — is preferred whenever one exists: it returns the source’s own text under its canonical URL, so the source node points at exactly the document the quote came from. Web fetches and search engines are the fallback, with a higher burden of scepticism: the URL is verified, the version date is read, the text is compared against any independent reference before it is trusted as the primary it claims to be.

item.title: how to do literate programming
item.description:
Prose is the primary artifact

rule
a literate program is first and foremost a piece of writing, written in the :: bullet form of the form of body text.
  • how: the bullets carry the full reasoning — problem, solution, and motivation.
  • how: a code block is an inline translation of a bullet’s claim, rendering the technical form of what the bullet already stated.
rule
a code block sits a glance away from the bullet it translates.
  • why: readers’ attention is narrow.
  • ideal: the reader sees the motivating bullet and the whole associated block without scrolling.
  • how: long code is split with noweb to show only the fragment relevant to the bullet at hand.
rule
the why lives in the paragraph that motivates the block, never in a code comment.
  • why: the why is never translated, so no code block can hold it.
  • why: a comment carrying a why — a system state, a design constraint, a justification of structure — is prose stranded in the wrong file, invisible to the narrative reader and out of context for the code reader.
  • scope: what remains in code is at most a one-liner annotating the line below.
check
remove all code blocks mentally, and the remaining text still forms a coherent and complete narrative.
  • why: this is what makes the document literate — code and prose interleaved, not inserted side by side.
  • how: a gap means either a paragraph is missing or an existing paragraph was paraphrasing a block rather than advancing the reasoning, and the section is rewritten accordingly.
  • how: a neutral agent reads the prose-only version and judges whether the narrative fulfills the stated need.
    • why: tests give a binary signal and prose coherence does not, so that reading is a stronger signal than code-level tests alone.

The reader’s flow is sacred

rule
the reader glides through the bullets uninterrupted, glancing at a code block to see how a bullet is concretely coded.
  • how: everything else — detours, meta-commentary, secondary justifications — is removed.
  • how: something valuable that breaks the flow — a technical derivation, a self-contained construction whose result the narrative will consume — moves to an annex, linked from the main narrative where its result is used.
  • rule: the shorter the sentence, the better it serves flow.
    • why: the longer a sentence, the more its message dilutes, and a convoluted clause already costs a glance back.
  • rule: a block is taken in at a glance, around thirty lines at most.
    • why: past that the reader loses the thread between the sentence that motivated the block and the code that is supposed to translate it.
    • how: the block splits along the seams the prose already has, each responsibility that was introduced as a distinct idea becoming its own block with a sentence of motivation just before, and noweb reassembles the pieces at tangle time.
    • how: a block that resists splitting means the prose has collapsed several ideas into one, so the prose is expanded first and the block splits naturally.
  • rule: a short conversational line stays when it names something the reader is already feeling.
    • why: a line like “let’s see what this gives”, just before a block that produces something visible, synchronizes the prose with the reader’s impatience to leave abstraction and see a concrete result, pacing the flow rather than interrupting it.
    • how: a line that introduces new content instead is a paragraph in disguise, and is expanded or cut.
rule
an ungrounded name breaks the flow wherever it appears.
  • why: the reading flow does not care which fence a name sits behind.
  • scope: this holds everywhere the reader’s eyes go — prose, comments, docstrings, function names, variable names, symbols, any identifier in any form.
  • rule: a new term enters the document where the document has just laid out what motivates it.
    • why: referring to a concept the reader has not yet met forces them to suspend reading, which breaks flow as surely as a detour.
    • how: reordering fixes it — the grounding sentence first, then the term that names what was just established.
    • how: when the structure constrains the sequence, the reference itself is deferred — name a more general concept the reader already has, and let the specific term arrive when its time comes.
    • how: where a forward-reference to a code-level term — a field, a function, a class — hides a readback, removing the term fixes both at once.
      • why: the prose was reaching for the implementation when it should have been naming the need.
  • rule: a reference in the exported flow is grounded in the exported flow.
    • why: content kept out of what the reader will read does not exist for that reader, so grounding that lives only there leaves the reference ungrounded forever.
    • how: either the grounding moves into the export, or the reference leaves it.
rule
prose carries the reasoning a picture cannot state — the motivation, the texture, the judgment.
rule
prose stops re-describing what a picture states better.
  • why: a picture delivers in one glance what a paragraph hands over clause by clause for the reader to reassemble.
rule
flow is more than the absence of friction.
  • rule: the reader feels the writer’s thrill, pulled forward by the chain of reasoning and eager to find out how it resolves.
    • why: a document that is technically clear but emotionally flat loses readers as surely as one that breaks flow with detours.
  • rule: a document is a story, not a recitation.
    • why: stakes, a tension building toward a result and a payoff at the end are what carry rigorous content through.
    • why: substance without narrative rarely lands, and style is what makes the logic count.
rule
a concept described elsewhere is one click away.
  • how: external definitions and references link out, and sections link to each other inside the note.
  • scope: exported content links only to exported content.
  • rule: a document whose outline has grown too long to hold in the head carries a table of contents.
    • why: the whole structure is then visible at a glance and every section is one click away.
    • how: in org-mode, a #+TOC: headlines N directive placed where the overview belongs, or #+OPTIONS: toc:t to let the exporter render one.
    • scope: a short note with two or three sections does without it.

Code blocks are not repeated in the export

rule
a code block appears in the export only when the prose talks about it.
  • why: this follows from the reader’s flow — re-showing a block the reader has already seen, because the next block depends on it, adds nothing to the reading.
  • why: the dependency is resolved at tangle time, invisibly to the reader.
  • scope: repetition is justified when seeing the surrounding code genuinely helps the reading.

Prose states the what, the how, and the why

The why

rule
the why is always a real one, traced back to a constraint, a measurement, or a decision someone actually made.
  • why: it is the one thing prose alone carries, and the easiest to fake — a plausible-sounding justification reads almost exactly like a real one.
  • why: a gap in the why is an honest signal that something still needs establishing, and a fabricated why hides that signal and ships a lie in its place.
  • how: a reason that is not known is said to be unknown, asked about, or discussed with whoever can settle it.
rule
a sentence whose only job is to make a paragraph sound complete is removed, not polished.

What earns a block

rule
a block exists only where the prose has made it necessary.
  • why: a block the prose did not lead to means a piece of reasoning is missing.
  • how: the why, the reason for the choice, stays in prose, untranslated.
  • how: the what, the desired behavior, is translated into a test.
  • how: the how, the chosen technical approach, is translated into code.
  • rule: prose states the problem or need, never a readback of the code.
    • rule: a what is never stated without its why.
    • why: prose that paraphrases the block is duplication, not justification, and a document listing “this does X, that does Y” hands over facts no one asked for.
    • how: the document moves in a single register — I need to meet this objective, so I will do this, and so I will do it this way — need, then intent, then technique.
    • scope: where the gap between intent and form is wide enough that a short readback bridges it, the readback earns its place as a translation aside.
  • scope: this binds the reading, not the source — tangle scaffolding lives invisibly, usually in :noexport: sections or marked :exports none, and needs no motivating prose because it is not read.
rule
the reading flow is the only criterion.
  • rule: it decides how prose and code are sliced against each other.
    • scope: one block per symbol, several symbols per block, several blocks per symbol are all legitimate.
    • how: the slicing has failed when the reader pauses on a function and asks “wait, what is this for? I was reading about something abstract and I don’t see the connection.”
    • how: boilerplate — every getter and setter of a Java bean, say — does not earn a sentence each.
      • why: that would drown the reader in motivation no one needed.
    • how: a block dropping several unrelated functions under a single vague paragraph calls either for more sentences or for splitting the block, whichever restores the flow.
      • why: it leaves the reader unmoored.
  • rule: it decides where vocabulary lives — the states a field can take, the thresholds that govern behavior and the constants that pace the system are named in prose, not in a type comment listing valid values, a magic number setting a tempo, or a literal fixing a bound.

Where blocks sit

rule
the test, the what, comes before the code, the how.
  • why: that is how we talk to each other — the desired behavior first, then the technique used to achieve it.
  • how: the prose states what is needed and what we are going to do — “we need the list to reject a duplicate,” “so we block creation” — and the block just below is that need made visible, code that happens to be a test.
    • why: the word test barely surfaces in the reading, and the reader meets a promised behavior and, right under it, the code that pins it down.
  • how: a test standing apart as a separate paragraph, not flowing from an explicit assertion in the prose, means a sentence is missing from the narrative.
  • scope: test-specific machinery — a tricky fixture, an unusual harness step — earns a sentence only when it is genuinely hard to follow, which is rare.
rule
a block is laid out against the prose that promises it.
  • rule: each prose paragraph promises one what, and the test block below it checks that promise.
    • why: a test block checking several whats under a single paragraph breaks the prose flow, and the reader cannot trace which sentence promised what the test is checking.
  • rule: a paragraph promising a what sits above the block that actually pins it.
    • why: when a block is only a step — it cannot fail unless an earlier one fails with it — the promise it appears to pin is pinned upstream, so prose that named it here has sent the reader to the wrong paragraph.
  • rule: each what stays a visible block in the feature chapter that motivated it, tagged with the session it serves via noweb (:noweb-ref triage-body).
rule
the sessions come first, in a chapter of their own.
  • why: the reader meets what the program is for before meeting its parts, and a block that is only a limb of a session cannot be read until the session binding it has been.
── chapter "Use cases", first in the note ────────────────────────
Prose: "the triager starts from the unsorted pile, narrows to what
        per is sorting, then works photo by photo — retagging,
        redating, filing"

  [wrapper — :noweb-ref tests
     @testcase
     def test_triage_a_morning(page):
         <<triage-body>>]

── feature chapter "Searching and filtering" ─────────────────────
Prose: "a label narrows the grid to the photos carrying it"

  [block — :noweb-ref triage-body
     type the label, commit, assert only those photos remain]

── feature chapter "The lightbox" ────────────────────────────────
Prose: "a wrong date is fixed on the photo itself"

  [block — :noweb-ref triage-body
     open the photo, edit its date, assert the grid re-orders]

Prose: "a duplicate in the list would make the tally incoherent,
        so we block creation and display an error message"

  [test — translates "we block and display a message"]
  [code — translates "we validate the list and expose a createError getter"]

What a test may reach

rule
every test exercises the program the way the final user does — same surfaces, same gestures, same outputs.
  • why: the closer the test’s path matches the user’s, the more its green bar means the promised behavior actually holds.
  • rule: the code carries nothing that exists solely for the test.
    • why: a data-testid, a hidden hook, a selector or attribute that exists only so a test can reach an element is a path no human will ever take, and the final user never reads a test id.
    • how: the test reaches for the handles the user has — the visible label, the role, the rendered text.
    • how: when the program turns out hard to test that way the difficulty is real information, and the fix belongs in the design.
      • why: usually the interface is just as unclear to the user.

Translation asides

rule
where the intent is clear but its shape in code is surprising, a short paragraph acts as a translator’s note — “we want X, but in code this is written as Y because Z”.
  • scope: this explains the gap between intent and form, not what the code does.
  • how: such asides should be rare.
  • how: an aside is clearly identifiable as such, introduced by something like “In practice,” or “Under the hood,”.
  • how: an aside that grows beyond its role, explaining more than the translation gap, moves to an annex the prose points at with a short link.
    • why: it would otherwise break the reader’s flow.
rule
needing an aside is read as a diagnostic before it is written.
  • why: sometimes it reflects a genuine gap between what human language and code can express, which is what the aside is for.
  • why: it can also reveal that the code is poorly organized, the surprising shape that needs a translator’s note simply being the wrong shape.
  • how: where the shape is wrong the code is refactored rather than papered over with an aside.
    • why: the structure of the code is not bound to the structure of the prose — noweb reassembles the pieces at tangle time, so the code can be carved along its own joints.
Prose: "we want the getters to behave as real properties"

  Under the hood, this means using defineProperty rather than Object.assign,
  which does not copy accessors.

  [code — translates this technical constraint]

Rewrite, don’t patch

rule
when something forces the document to change — a bug, an oversight, a change of mind, a breaking change in an upstream library, a refactor that obsoletes an earlier choice — the affected prose section is rewritten so it reads as if the issue never existed.
  • why: adding a test and an explanatory paragraph describing the mitigation leaves a visible scar rather than restoring the narrative.
  • why: a scar interrupts the reader’s flow just as surely as a detour does.
  • how: the result is not a narrative that fixes something but one that was always correct, betraying no trace of the path that led to it.
rule
a scar is retrospective — a trace of a revision already applied, a debate already settled.
  • how: the distinguishing test is tense — a sentence describing a fix already made is a scar and is rewritten, one naming an open question the reader should know about is a caveat and is kept.
  • scope: prospective language is not a scar — honest framing of a value still to validate empirically, of an explicit test plan, or of a guard-rail against a tempting wrong path.
Scar — rewrite:
  "initially at 120 mm/s, since revised to 60 mm/s for volumetric flow"

Caveat — keep:
  "clearance at 0.5 mm — to adjust by trial if the real fit is too loose"
rule
when reasoning leaves the code — a justification moved to prose, a constraint absorbed into a cleaner design — the code that only carried it leaves as well.
  • how: an empty body, a one-armed conditional, a vestigial helper is each a fragment whose work now lives elsewhere.
  • why: the artifact then reads as if neither prose nor code remembered the revision.

item.title: Comment ecrire une note de litterature juridique
item.description:
Table des matières
  • Balayer avant de conclure : la complétude n’est pas la fidélité
  • Vérifier en droit : la date, le visa, l’ordre, le poids
  • Les faits ne sont pas dans les sources
  • Le périmètre fait partie de la réponse
  • Le piège : la présomption prétorienne concurrente
  • Permalink

Balayer avant de conclure : la complétude n’est pas la fidélité

Un audit qui vérifie que chaque verbatim et chaque visa cités sont exacts contrôle la fidélité de la note. Il ne dit RIEN de sa complétude. Une note peut être irréprochable sur ce qu’elle cite et néanmoins survendre sa thèse parce qu’elle ignore une autorité qu’elle n’a pas cherchée. L’audit de fidélité et l’audit de complétude sont distincts et tous deux nécessaires.

item.title: how to do literate programming for the web
item.description:
Table of Contents
  • Show the element itself
  • CSS renders to a picture, so show the picture
  • Frame a live component beside the prose that builds it
  • Animate the interaction
  • Permalink

Show the element itself

The general guide says a diagram beats a paragraph wherever the content is visual. On the web the bar is higher still: the content is not merely visual, it is the live artifact itself, and the export can hold it. So whenever the prose introduces something the reader will see or touch — a styled element, a widget, a page fragment — show that thing, rendered, right there.
